doc_name: Murder of Sagar Sarowar and Meherun Runi
text: The murder of Sagar Sarowar and Meherun Runi, a well-known married Bangladeshi journalist couple, remains an unsolved double murder case that occurred on 11 February 2012 when they were stabbed to death in their apartment in the West Raja Bazar neighbourhood of Dhaka. The couple, who lived with their five-year-old son, were killed sometime between 2 and 5 a.m., shortly after Sarowar returned from work at Maasranga Television, and before the dawn Fajr prayer. Their son discovered their bodies around 7 a.m. and called Runi’s mother, prompting the crime scene to become active around 11 a.m. The apartment showed signs of being searched, with possessions scattered and a kitchen window grill cut to approximately 1.8 feet, too small for an adult to pass through. The investigation was jointly managed by the Bangladesh Police’s Tejgaon Thana and the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), with high-level officials including Inspector General Hassan Mahmood Khandker and Dhaka Metropolitan Police Commissioner Benajir Ahmed present. A total of 14 teams were deployed, and the case attracted significant political and media attention, with politicians such as Home Minister Sahara Khatun promising arrests within 48 hours. The autopsies, conducted at Dhaka Medical College, revealed multiple stab wounds, with Sarowar receiving the most, and possibly three knives used; no viscera test was performed initially, leading to criticism, and later exhumations were carried out under RAB supervision with samples sent to the United States for DNA analysis. The RAB identified 8 suspects in October 2012, arrested seven around 9 October 2012, and made another arrest in February 2013, though no motive was ever publicly disclosed. The families and journalists doubted the suspects' involvement, and a 2013 report found that DNA from the suspects did not match the samples. The investigation was declared stalled after two months, with the High Court reassigning it to RAB in April 2012 and establishing a monitoring committee including journalists, lawyers, human rights activists, and academics. Despite efforts, the probe report was delayed 91 times by 24 August 2022, and no progress has been made after a decade. The case drew international attention due to Sarowar’s prior work for Deutsche Welle and the involvement of journalists and press freedom organisations. The murder is believed to have been pre-meditated by someone who knew the victims, with reports suggesting possible motives related to their reporting on energy corruption and minority rights. Rumors circulated that the Awami League and India were involved, and leaked call records allegedly showed the killing was ordered by then-Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. The case unified separate journalist organisations, and the families, along with Reporters Without Borders and Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh, called for an international commission. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina visited the family, promised justice, and criticized journalists for protests and for interviewing the son, while also claiming that more journalists were killed during opposition rule. The murder is part of a broader pattern, with Bangladesh having 12 confirmed journalist killings since 1992 and only three convictions, ranking 11th on the CPJ’s Impunity Index. In 2015, Bangladesh ranked 146th out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders Press Freedom Index. The couple is buried in the Azimpur graveyard in old Dhaka, a well-known Muslim burial site. The son, who was interviewed by journalists, became a central figure in media coverage, raising ethical concerns. The crime scene was visited by numerous political figures, including BNP leader Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, who criticized the lack of law and order, and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who both praised and criticized journalists. The case remains open, with no suspects convicted.

doc_name: Murder of Sagar Sarowar and Meherun Runi
text: The double murder of the high-profile media couple Sagar and Runi, which occurred in Bangladesh, drew widespread attention and outrage. Journalists covered the incident extensively, with the 5-year-old son of the victims, who discovered the bodies and called for help, frequently featured in news reports. This raised ethical concerns, particularly in light of the 2010 UNESCO report "Ethical Reporting on and for Children." Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina criticized the media for interviewing the boy and for destroying evidence. The murder united journalists across Bangladesh, leading to the re-unification of the Bangladesh Federal Union of Journalists and the Dhaka Union of Journalists, which had been separate since 1992. They organized rallies, hunger strikes, panel discussions, and lobbying efforts. Key events included a rally on 12 February, a nationwide human chain and rally on 22 February, a one-hour hunger strike and work stoppage on 27 February 2012, further hunger strikes on 1 March and 23 December, a grand rally around 18 March 2012 in various districts, and a sit-in on 8 April. After Home Minister Sahara Khatun assured them police would produce results soon, journalists stood down. On 5 June 2012, they submitted written correspondence to the Speaker supporting laws to protect journalists. On 26 June 2012, they marched toward the prime minister's office. Journalists held panel discussions on the case, including on its first anniversary, with participants such as Monjurul Ahsan Bulbul, A B M Musa, Golam Sarowar, Shahed Chowdhury, Iqbal Sobhan Chowdhury, Ruhul Amin Gazi, Kamal Uddin Sabuj, and Syed Abdal Ahmad. When Home Minister Muhiuddin Khan Alamgir made unfounded remarks about the families' lack of cooperation, he withdrew his statement after journalists protested. In Germany, Bangladeshi expatriates, Germans, and citizens from other European countries protested in Frankfurt and Bonn, forming a human chain around the UN building in Bonn to draw attention to the stalled investigation and seek action from the UN and EU. UNESCO's Irina Bokova called the murder "an intolerable attack on the profession and on the fundamental human right for freedom of expression." The International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) stated that the murder threatened progress in journalist safety. Information Minister Hasanul Haq Inu said the killing was "disgraceful for democracy" and that the government's duty was to remove it. After one year with no progress, Nowsher Alam Roman, Runi's brother, expressed ongoing agony, frustration, and fear, criticizing the government for fake sympathy and broken promises. The IFJ-Asia Pacific echoed this, lamenting the slow investigation and lack of motive. The Daily Star editorial noted skepticism about authorities' ability to deliver a credible conclusion. The Dhaka Courier's end-of-year editorial stated that the murder remained unresolved and that the government had failed to provide a satisfactory explanation, citing salacious motives and names of prominent figures. Saleha Manir, Sagar Sarowar's mother, asked at a rally, "How many days more will I have to count to see full 48 hours?" Home Minister Sahara Khatun had previously ordered law enforcement to arrest the murderers within 48 hours. BNP leader Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir claimed the country was becoming a "slaughter ground" and that there was no law or rule of law. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina remarked, "Government can't guard one's bedroom."
